title: \(C(K)\)-spaces with few operators relative to posets
author: Antonio Acuaviva
abstract: Extending a method developed by Koszmider and Laustsen for constructing \(C(K)\)-spaces we produce families of \(C(K)\)-spaces with few operators relative to a partially ordered set \(\mathcal{P}\). Using these spaces, we construct new \(C(K)\)-spaces whose closed operator ideals can be completely classified. Additionally, we use these spaces to resolve some questions regarding automatic continuity.

1.

Introduction and main results

−

The question of which kinds of operators must exist on a Banach space has a long and deep history. In the separable case, we find the seminal works of Gowers and Maurey . They constructed a space in which every operator is a strictly singular perturbation of a scalar multiple of the identity, providing a negative solution to the unconditional basic sequence problem. These ideas have had a profound impact on Banach space theory, yielding counterexamples to numerous open problems; see for a comprehensive survey of these developments. This cycle of ideas culminated in the landmark resolution of the “scalar-plus-compact” problem by Argyros and Haydon , which has since inspired numerous new research directions.

However, the first construction of a Banach space with “few operators” was not achieved in the separable setting. Shelah constructed a non-separable Banach space on which every operator is a separable perturbation of a scalar multiple of the identity. Shelah’s original construction relied on an additional set-theoretical axiom, \(\Diamond\), but this was later removed in the work of Shelah and Steprāns . This line of research was further developed by Argyros and Tolias , who constructed a dual space with this property, and by Wark , who produced a reflexive and a uniformly convex space with the aforementioned property.

All the previously mentioned Banach spaces have very complex definitions; in contrast, spaces of continuous functions over compact Hausdorff spaces \(C(K)\) are among the simplest Banach spaces one can define. In this direction, in 2005, Koszmider , assuming the Continuum Hypothesis \((\mathsf{CH})\), constructed a scattered locally compact Hausdorff space \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) such that the corresponding space \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) admits as few operators as possible, in the sense that every operator \(T:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) is of the form \(T=\lambda\operatorname{Id}+S\), where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\) (the scalar field, either \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\)) and \(S\) factors through \(c_{0}\). The dependence on \((\mathsf{CH})\) was later removed in the work of Koszmider and Laustsen . Both arguments rely on the construction of a locally compact Hausdorff space induced by a carefully chosen almost disjoint family.

Let \(\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) denote the set of all infinite subsets of the natural numbers. A family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) is called almost disjoint if for every distinct \(A,B\in\mathcal{A}\), the intersection \(A\cap B\) is finite. An almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) induces a locally compact Hausdorff space \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\), usually referred to as a \(\Psi\)-space, Isbell–Mrówka space, AU-compactum, or Mrówka space; see Definition 4.1 for details.

These spaces were first introduced into Banach space theory by Johnson and Lindenstrauss, who used a renorming of \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\)-spaces to construct counterexamples concerning weakly compactly generated Banach spaces .

Mrówka spaces have been used to construct several examples of exotic Banach spaces in recent years. Notably, Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón constructed an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) provides a counterexample to the complemented subspace problem for \(C(K)\)-spaces . Remarkably, de Hevia, Martínez-Cervantes, Salguero-Alarcón, and Tradacete have subsequently shown that this space also serves as a counterexample to the complemented subspace problem for Banach lattices . We have recently extended these results by showing that a similar construction shows that the class of Banach lattices is not primary .

As previously mentioned, these spaces were also used by Koszmider and Laustsen to build a Banach space of continuous functions with as few operators as possible. It is within this context that our work is situated. We build on their ideas to construct new \(C(K)\)-spaces with interesting properties. In particular, these spaces allow us to resolve some of the questions left open in . The following theorem summarises our main results in this direction, where \(\wp(\mathfrak{c})\) denotes the power set of the continuum, equipped with the order structure given by inclusion of sets.

Suppose that \(\mathcal{P}\) is a partially ordered set which admits an order embedding into \(\wp(\mathfrak{c})\). Then there exist a collection \((\mathcal{A}_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) of uncountable, almost disjoint families \(\mathcal{A}_{t}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) and a collection of isometric algebra homomorphisms \(\iota_{s,t}:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{t}})\) for \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\) with \(s\leq t\) such that:

  1. (a)

    \(\iota_{s,s}\) is the identity on \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\), and \(\iota_{s,t}\iota_{r,s}=\iota_{r,t}\) for all \(r\leq s\leq t\).

  2. (b)

    Let \(T:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{t}})\) be an operator for some \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\). Then

    • –

      if \(s\leq t\), then \(T=\lambda\iota_{s,t}+S\), where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\) and \(S\) is an operator that factors through \(c_{0}\),

    • –

      if \(s\not\leq t\), then \(T\) factors through \(c_{0}\).

This theorem has many interesting consequences. In particular, every partially ordered set \(\mathcal{P}\) with \(|\mathcal{P}|\leq\mathfrak{c}\) order-embeds into \((\wp(\mathfrak{c}),\subseteq)\): the map \(t\mapsto\{s\in\mathcal{P}:s\leq t\}\) embeds \(\mathcal{P}\) into \((\wp(\mathcal{P}),\subseteq)\), and, after identifying \(\mathcal{P}\) with a subset of \(\mathfrak{c}\), this gives an embedding into \((\wp(\mathfrak{c}),\subseteq)\).

Thus, for example, suppose that we let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a set of cardinality continuum with the trivial order, that is, \(s\leq t\) if and only if \(s=t\). In that case, it gives continuum many non-isomorphic \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\)-spaces with few operators, thereby yielding a large collection of non-isomorphic \(C(K)\)-spaces for which the complemented subspaces and the closed operator ideals are completely classified, see and respectively. Moreover, as an easy consequence, we recover the existence of \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\) distinct isomorphism classes of such spaces, a result previously obtained, by different methods, in .

There are \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\) pairwise non-isomorphic spaces of the form \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is an almost disjoint family of cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\).

Proof.Fold proof

Choose an antichain \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq\wp(\mathfrak{c})\) of cardinality \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\). For example, identify \(\mathfrak{c}\) with \(\mathfrak{c}\times 2\), and for each function \(\varepsilon:\mathfrak{c}\to 2\) define

\(P_{\varepsilon}=\{(\xi,\varepsilon(\xi)):\xi<\mathfrak{c}\}.\)

Then \(\mathcal{P}=\{P_{\varepsilon}:\varepsilon\in 2^{\mathfrak{c}}\}\) is an antichain in \((\wp(\mathfrak{c}),\subseteq)\) of cardinality \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\).

Applying Theorem 1.1 to this partially ordered set, we obtain almost disjoint families \((\mathcal{A}_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) and spaces \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{t}})\) for each \(t\in\mathcal{P}\). We claim that these spaces are pairwise non-isomorphic.

Indeed, let \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\) with \(s\neq t\). Since \(\mathcal{P}\) is an antichain, we have \(s\not\leq t\). Hence every operator from \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\) into \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{t}})\) factors through \(c_{0}\), and in particular it has separable range. Thus, it cannot be an isomorphism, and therefore the spaces are not isomorphic. ∎

The true significance of the above theorem is that we can use the spaces \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) as building blocks to construct a plethora of \(C(K)\)-spaces displaying a rich variety of complemented subspaces and lattices of closed operator ideals. From this point onward, any reference to an operator ideal, or to lattices of operator ideals, will be understood to refer exclusively to closed operator ideals.

Analysing the closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is intimately connected to identifying which unital Banach algebras can be isomorphic to the quotient algebra

\(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\)

for some almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\), where \(\mathscr{X}\) denotes the ideal of operators with separable range. The following proposition, whose proof is essentially the same as that of , makes this connection explicit.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) be an almost disjoint family. The ideal \(\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) of compact operators is the smallest non-zero closed ideal of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) and if \(\varphi:\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\to\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) denotes the quotient map, then

\(\mathscr{J}\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathscr{J})\)

is a lattice isomorphism between the lattice of closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) and the closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) strictly larger than \(\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\).

Let \(\mathfrak{J}\) denote the lattice of closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\), then the previous proposition can be succinctly described by saying that the lattice of closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is given by

\(\{0\}\subsetneq\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\subsetneq\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{J}).\)

It follows that the problem of understanding closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) reduces to understanding the closed ideals of the quotient algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\). Consequently, we focus on determining which unital Banach algebras can be realised as such quotients. The following terminology will allow us to state the main construction concisely.

  • •

    Let \((\mathscr{C}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a sequence of normed algebras. The normed direct product of the sequence \((\mathscr{C}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is defined as

    \(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}:=\left\{a=(a_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}:a_{n}\in\mathscr{C}_{n},\hskip 5.0pt\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left\lVert a_{n}\right\rVert<\infty\right\},\)

    equipped with the norm

    \(\left\lVert a\right\rVert:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\left\lVert a_{n}\right\rVert,\)

    and with addition and multiplication defined component-wise.

  • •

    Set

    \(\displaystyle\mathfrak{A}=\{0\}\cup\{\mathbb{M}_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\cup\{\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}):|\mathcal{P}|<\infty\}\cup\{\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0}):\mathcal{P}\text{ countable}\}\cup\{\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\},\)

    where \(\mathbb{M}_{n}\) denotes the algebra of \(n\times n\) matrices, equipped with the norm it inherits under the identification with \(\mathscr{B}(\ell_{\infty}^{n})\), \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) is the incidence algebra induced by a finite poset \(\mathcal{P}\), and \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\) is the \(c_{0}\)-incidence algebra induced by a countable poset \(\mathcal{P}\) (see Definitions 6.4 and 6.9 for details of this terminology).

Let \((\mathscr{C}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathfrak{A}\). Then there exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) and a short exact sequence

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

which splits strongly. Furthermore, the continuous right inverse \(\rho\) may be chosen to be an isometry, and \(\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert=1\) whenever \(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\neq\{0\}\).

Here “splits strongly” is understood in the sense of Definition 2.2; in particular, there is a continuous algebra homomorphism \(\rho\colon\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\to\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) such that \(\theta\circ\rho\) is the identity map on \(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\). Equivalently, if zero factors are allowed, the one-factor case can be viewed as the product with \(\mathscr{C}_{1}=\mathscr{C}\) and \(\mathscr{C}_{n}=\{0\}\) for \(n\geq 2\).

The previous theorem provides a partial answer to . In particular, since we can obtain the finite product of matrix algebras, Wedderburn’s structure theorem automatically gives the following.

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a finite-dimensional, semi-simple complex algebra. Then there exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is isomorphic to \(\mathscr{C}\).

Using these families, we can prove the following result regarding automatic continuity.

There exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that there is a discontinuous surjective algebra homomorphism

\(\Psi\colon\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\longrightarrow\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K}),\)

where \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\) denotes the algebra of upper-triangular \(2\times 2\) scalar matrices. Consequently, there exist a compact scattered Hausdorff space \(K\) of Cantor–Bendixson height at most three and a discontinuous surjective algebra homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))\) onto \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\).

The proof is deferred to Subsection 8.1. This answers a question raised by the author and a question of Koszmider and Laustsen . It also gives a genuinely new example and method, different from the one of Read , of a Banach space \(X\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) admits a discontinuous homomorphism into a Banach algebra (without additional set-theoretic assumptions).

Theorem 1.8 does not control derivations from the same operator algebra. Following the arguments in , we believe that, under \((\mathsf{CH})\), it should be possible to construct an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\) such that every derivation from \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is continuous while the algebra admits a discontinuous homomorphism into a Banach algebra. Establishing these two properties simultaneously would require a substantially longer argument.

We want to highlight that there are extremely few \(C(K)\)-spaces for which the lattice of closed operator ideals has been fully classified. In fact, even the number of such ideals is known only for the spaces listed below. To the best of our knowledge, these are:

  • •

    \(c_{0}(\Gamma)\) for any set \(\Gamma\); in this case, the lattice of closed operator ideals was classified by Gohberg, Markus and Feldman in the case \(\Gamma=\mathbb{N}\) and extended to uncountable sets by Daws . This lattice is well-ordered and consists of the ideals of \(\kappa\)-compact operators. An alternative description of this ideal lattice was also given by Johnson, Kania and Schechtman .

  • •

    \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) where \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) is the space constructed by Koszmider and Laustsen so that \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) admits few operators. In this case, Kania and Kochanek , showed that the lattice of closed ideals is

    \(\{0\}\subsetneq\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\subsetneq\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\subsetneq\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})).\)

    A similar conclusion holds for \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})^{n}\cong C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}\times\{1,\dots,n\})\) for any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\).

  • •

    \(C_{0}(\omega\times K_{\mathcal{A}})\) where again \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) is the space built by Koszmider and Laustsen. We recently showed that the lattice of closed operator ideals consists of five linearly ordered ideals .

It is interesting to note that all the previously known examples have a linearly ordered lattice and thus a unique maximal ideal. Applying Theorem 1.5, together with Proposition 1.3, allows us to produce multiple \(C(K)\)-spaces whose lattices of closed operator ideals behave very differently, using the fact that the ideal structure of incidence algebras is essentially known .

In particular, we can obtain ideal lattices that are not linearly ordered and with many maximal ideals. In fact, for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), the \(n\times n\) upper triangular matrices have precisely \(n\) maximal ideals, and thus we can find an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) has \(n\) maximal ideals. We refer to Subsection 8.2 for a more detailed account of possible ideals.

Lastly, we would like to emphasise that, to obtain spaces of operators on \(C(K)\)-spaces with more than one maximal ideal, one must consider non-separable \(C(K)\)-spaces. We refer to Section 3 for details, where we show the following.

For the unique maximal ideal assertion, assume K is nonempty.

Let \(C(K)\) be separable. Then \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))\) has a unique maximal ideal. Moreover, there exists some \(n\in\{2,3\}\) such that the space of operators on any separable \(C(K)\)-space never has exactly \(n\) non-trivial closed ideals.

Correction in this reading edition

K is understood to be nonempty in the unique maximal ideal assertion. The zero algebra has no proper maximal ideal.

In contrast, in the non-separable setting, as previously mentioned, a result of Daws shows that, for any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), the algebra \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(\aleph_{n-1}))\) admits exactly \(n\) non-trivial closed ideals. This motivates us to pose the following question.

For which \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(n\geq 1\), does there exist an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that the operator algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) contains exactly \(n\) non-trivial closed ideals?

We note that, by Theorem 1.5, a significant subset of the natural numbers can be realised as the number of non-trivial closed ideals of algebras of the form \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\). This is explored further in Subsection 8.2, where we give a general procedure for producing such numbers from finite incidence algebras and finite products of admissible quotient algebras.

We conjecture that, in fact, every natural number arises in this way, but a new procedure to build specific algebras as quotients may be needed.

2.

Organisation and notation

−

All normed spaces and algebras are over the scalar field \(\mathbb{K}\), either the real or complex numbers, and we adhere to standard notational conventions. For a compact Hausdorff space \(\Omega\), we denote by \(C(\Omega)\) the space of continuous functions \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{K}\). Similarly, for a locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\), we denote by \(C_{0}(K)\) the space of continuous functions on \(K\) that vanish at infinity, that is, continuous functions \(f:K\to\mathbb{K}\) such that the set \(\{k\in K:|f(k)|\geq\varepsilon\}\) is compact for each \(\varepsilon>0\).

The term operator will refer to a bounded linear map between normed spaces. For two Banach spaces \(X\) and \(Y\), we denote by \(\mathscr{B}(X,Y)\) the space of operators between \(X\) and \(Y\). In the case \(X=Y\), we simply write \(\mathscr{B}(X)\). When referring to ideals, we will always mean two-sided closed ideals.

Furthermore, whenever we consider the finite direct sum of \(n\) Banach spaces, it is understood implicitly that the sum is equipped with the \(\ell_{\infty}^{n}\) norm. We will denote by \(\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) the set of all infinite subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\). Finally, given a sequence \((a_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) and a set \(A\in\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\), we write \(\lim_{n\in A}a_{n}\) to mean \(\lim_{k\to\infty}a_{n_{k}}\), where \((n_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\) is the increasing enumeration of \(A\).

We recall the following standard terminology for Banach algebras.

A sequence of Banach algebra homomorphisms

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{I}\xlongrightarrow{\jmath}\mathscr{B}\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\mathscr{C}\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

is called short exact if \(\jmath\) is injective, \(\theta\) is surjective and \(\ker\theta=\jmath(\mathscr{I})\). In the applications below, \(\jmath\) will be the inclusion map, and we shall identify \(\mathscr{I}\) with its image in \(\mathscr{B}\).

A short exact sequence

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{I}\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\mathscr{C}\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

is called strongly split if there is a continuous algebra homomorphism \(\rho\colon\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{B}\) such that \(\theta\circ\rho\) is the identity map on \(\mathscr{C}\). In this case, \(\rho\) is called a continuous right inverse for \(\theta\).

More specialised notation will be introduced as and when needed.

We give a brief overview of the structure of this paper. In Section 3, we discuss the separable \(C(K)\) case and show that separable \(C(K)\)-spaces always have a unique maximal ideal of operators. This explains why the later examples must be non-separable if one wants several maximal ideals. In Section 4, we introduce the notation and preliminary results needed for the proof of Theorem 1.1. In Subsection 4.1 we begin by recalling the definition of the topological spaces \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) induced by an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\), as well as some basic properties concerning separability. We then explore how to combine different \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\)-spaces to construct new spaces of this form, and explain how the inclusion \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) of almost disjoint families affects the relationship between the spaces \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) and \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\).

In Subsection 4.2, we describe how infinite matrices can be interpreted as acting between the spaces \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) and \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\). To do this, we adapt several definitions and results originally developed by Koszmider and Laustsen to the setting in which the domain and codomain differ. Readers already familiar with their work may wish to skip or only briefly skim this subsection, referring back to it as and when needed.

Lastly, Subsection 4.3 explains how to represent an operator \(T:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\) as an \(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\) matrix, and how this representation relates to the matrix theory discussed earlier. Readers familiar with the work of Koszmider and Laustsen will recognise most of the results presented here as natural extensions of ideas already developed in . Section 5 presents the proof of Theorem 1.1.

Finally, Section 6 introduces the concepts of incidence algebras and \(c_{0}\)-incidence algebras, and explains how these algebras can be realised as quotients by the ideal of separable-range operators. Section 7 contains the proof of Theorem 1.5. The paper concludes with Section 8. Subsection 8.1 proves the ZFC automatic-continuity result stated in Theorem 1.8, while Subsection 8.2 discusses possible quotient algebras and ideal counts and records the multiplicative nature of the construction.

3.

Operator ideals for separable \(C(K)\)-spaces

−

This section explains why the examples constructed later must be non-separable if one wants several maximal ideals. It is easy to build non-separable \(C(K)\)-spaces whose operator ideal lattice is not linearly ordered. For instance, since the algebras of operators on \(C([0,1])\) and on \(C(\omega_{1})\) each have a unique maximal ideal, one can verify that the algebra of operators on \(C([0,1])\oplus C(\omega_{1})\) has precisely two maximal ideals. However, a complete classification of the closed operator ideals on spaces of this kind appears to be out of reach. By contrast, in the separable \(C(K)\) setting there is always a unique maximal ideal, as we will see.

We shall use the following notation. For Banach spaces \(X\) and \(Y\), define

\(\mathcal{M}_{Y}(X)=\{T\in\mathscr{B}(X):I_{Y}\text{ does not factor through }T\}.\)

When \(X=Y\), this agrees with the notation introduced by Dosev and Johnson , namely \(\mathcal{M}_{X}(X)=\mathcal{M}_{X}\). We can now make the following observation, which appears to have gone unnoticed in the literature.

For every infinite ordinal \(\alpha\), the algebra of operators on \(C(\alpha)\) has a unique maximal ideal. In particular, if \(C(\alpha)\not\sim C(\xi\cdot n)\) for any uncountable regular cardinal \(\xi\) and \(n\in\mathbb{N},n\geq 2\) then the set \(\mathcal{M}_{C(\alpha)}(C(\alpha))\) is the unique maximal ideal of \(\mathscr{B}(C(\alpha))\).

Proof.Fold proof

First, assume that \(C(\alpha)\) is not isomorphic to \(C(\xi\cdot n)\) for any uncountable regular cardinal \(\xi\) and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(n\geq 2\). In this case, an inspection of the proof of the primariness of \(C(\alpha)\) by Benyamini and Alspach shows that if \(T,S\in\mathscr{B}(C(\alpha))\) are such that \(T+S=I_{C(\alpha)}\), then one of \(T\) or \(S\) factors the identity on \(C(\alpha)\) (in the case that \(\alpha\) is countable, this can also be seen from Wolfe’s proof of primariness ).

Indeed, for Cases I and II in the proof of , we can still invoke for any operator \(T\), not necessarily a projection. The assumption \(T+S=I_{C(\alpha)}\) is precisely what we need for arguing that we can assume \(X\) is \((c,1/10)\)-preserved with \(c\geq 1/2\) by either \(T\) or \(S\). After this, we can invoke to conclude that the operator, either \(T\) or \(S\), fixes a complemented copy of \(C_{0}(\alpha)\) and thus it factors the identity \(I_{C(\alpha)}\).

Cases III and IV follow in the same way, noting that the fact that \(P_{Y}\) and \(P_{Z}\) are projections is never actually used; the only essential point is that \(P_{Y}+P_{Z}=I_{C(\alpha)}\), which ensures that the operators \((c,1/20)\)-preserve the spaces \(X_{\delta}\) for some \(c\geq 1/2\).

Equivalently, the preceding argument shows that for every operator \(T\in\mathscr{B}(C(\alpha))\), we have

\(T\notin\mathcal{M}_{C(\alpha)}(C(\alpha))\quad\text{or}\quad I_{C(\alpha)}-T\notin\mathcal{M}_{C(\alpha)}(C(\alpha)).\)

It then follows from that \(\mathcal{M}_{C(\alpha)}(C(\alpha))\) is the unique maximal ideal in \(\mathscr{B}(C(\alpha))\).

Suppose now that \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\xi\cdot n)\cong\bigoplus_{j=1}^{n}C(\xi)\) for some uncountable regular cardinal \(\xi\) and integer \(n\geq 2\). By the previous argument, \(\mathscr{B}(C(\xi))\) admits a unique maximal ideal. Elementary arguments using the matrix representation of operators on direct sums then yield the uniqueness of a maximal ideal in this case.

By the classification theorem for spaces of continuous functions on ordinals —originally proved independently by Gul’ko and Kislyakov , and stated in the specific form used here in —these are all the possible cases up to isomorphism. ∎

The case \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\omega_{1})\), or more generally \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\omega_{\eta})\) where \(\eta\) is any ordinal such that \(\omega_{\eta}\) is a regular cardinal, was already shown by Kania and Laustsen , while the case \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\beta)\) for \(\beta\) a countable epsilon number, that is, a countable ordinal satisfying \(\omega^{\beta}=\beta\), was shown by Philip A. H. Brooker (unpublished).

We now pass from ordinal compacta to arbitrary separable \(C(K)\)-spaces.

Assume K is nonempty.

Let \(K\) be a compact metric space. Then \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))\) admits a unique maximal ideal.

Correction in this reading edition

K is nonempty here. The statement about a unique maximal ideal fails for the zero function space.

Proof.Fold proof

If \(K\) is finite, the result is trivial. Whenever \(K\) is countable and infinite, the classification theorem of Bessaga and Pełczyński gives \(C(K)\sim C(\alpha)\) for some infinite countable ordinal \(\alpha\). The result now follows from Proposition 3.1.

6.

Quotient algebras and operator ideals

−

We explore some consequences of Theorem 1.1 for the construction of \(C(K)\)-spaces whose closed operator ideals can be classified. For convenience, we present our result in slightly more general terms. We will need the following definition.

Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a partially ordered set. We say that a family \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) of Banach spaces has few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}\) if the following are satisfied for \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\):

  1. (a)

    \(X_{t}\) is not separable.

  2. (b)

    If \(s\leq t\) then there exists an isometric embedding \(\iota_{s,t}:X_{s}\to X_{t}\) so that every operator \(T:X_{s}\to X_{t}\) is of the form \(T=\lambda\iota_{s,t}+S\), where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\) and \(S\) has separable range. Furthermore, for every \(r\leq s\leq t\) we have \(\iota_{s,t}\iota_{r,s}=\iota_{r,t}\).

  3. (c)

    If \(s\not\leq t\), then every operator \(T:X_{s}\to X_{t}\) has separable range.

We think of the spaces \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) as being nested relative to the poset \(\mathcal{P}\). Accordingly, whenever we write \(X_{s}\subseteq X_{t}\) for \(s\leq t\), we implicitly identify \(X_{s}\) with its image \(\iota_{s,t}(X_{s})\subseteq X_{t}\).

In case (c), that is, whenever \(s\nleq t\), we adopt the convention of defining \(\iota_{s,t}=0\) to maintain consistency in the notation.

According to Theorem 1.1, for any poset \(\mathcal{P}\) of size at most the continuum, we can always find a family of non-separable \(C(K)\)-spaces which has few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}\). We recall that a poset \(\mathcal{P}\) is said to be locally finite if for any \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\) with \(s\leq t\), the interval \([s,t]=\{r\in\mathcal{P}:s\leq r\leq t\}\) is finite.

Let \((\mathcal{P},\leq)\) be a locally finite partially ordered set. The incidence algebra of \(\mathcal{P}\) is the algebra

\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})=\{f\colon\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{K}:f(s,t)=0\text{ for }s,t\in\mathcal{P}\text{ with }s\not\leq t\},\)

with the sum of functions and scalar multiplication defined pointwise. The product \(h=f\star g\) is defined via convolution

\(h(s,t)=\sum_{s\leq r\leq t}f(s,r)g(r,t).\)

For technical reasons, we will work with the incidence algebra on the poset with the opposite order \(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Observe that this algebra can be explicitly described in terms of the original order as

\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}})=\{f\colon\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{K}:f(s,t)=0\text{ for }s,t\in\mathcal{P}\text{ with }t\not\leq s\},\)

and the product becomes

\((f\star g)(s,t)=\sum_{t\leq r\leq s}f(s,r)g(r,t).\)

Incidence algebras were originally introduced by Rota to provide a general framework for inversion-type formulas and have since found multiple applications. Examples of incidence algebras include, among others, the algebra of \(n\times n\) upper-triangular matrices \(\mathbb{T}_{n}\), which is induced by the linearly ordered set of \(n\) elements.

We would like to point out that incidence algebras naturally carry a topology, given by pointwise convergence of functions. For \(\mathcal{P}\) finite, this topology coincides with the one induced by any norm. In this case, we will regard elements in \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) as operators on \((\mathbb{K}^{\mathcal{P}},\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\infty})\) and equip \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) with the operator norm. Specifically, \(f\in\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) acts on an element \(v\in\mathbb{K}^{\mathcal{P}}\) by

\((f\cdot v)(s)=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{P}}f(s,t)v(t).\)

Of special interest in our case is the fact that, with this topology understood, there is a procedure to determine the closed ideals of incidence algebras; see .

8.1.1.

Construction of the discontinuous homomorphism

The main difficulty in the first stage is to construct an unbounded functional on the off-diagonal block which is nevertheless compatible with multiplication by the two diagonal blocks. For this purpose, we construct finite-to-one maps \(f_{n}\colon D\to R\) and ultrafilters \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) such that all the pushforwards \(f_{n}(\mathcal{U})\) equal \(\mathcal{V}\), while distinct maps \(f_{n}\) and \(f_{m}\) disagree on a set belonging to \(\mathcal{U}\). Passing to an algebraic quotient and using a Hamel-basis extension then produces an unbounded functional \(L\) satisfying the required bimodule identities. These identities are precisely what makes the resulting map into \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\) multiplicative.

We write \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\) for the algebra of matrices

\(\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ 0&\gamma\end{pmatrix}\qquad(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{K}),\)

equipped with the operator norm inherited from \(\mathscr{B}(\ell_{\infty}^{2})\).

If \(\mathcal{U}\) is an ultrafilter on a set \(S\), define \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}\colon\ell_{\infty}(S)\to\mathbb{K}\) by

\(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)=\lim_{s\to\mathcal{U}}a(s)\qquad(a\in\ell_{\infty}(S)).\)

The limit is well defined because a closed disk in \(\mathbb{K}\) is compact, and continuity of the scalar operations shows that \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}\) is a norm-one character. Namely, \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}\) denotes the character given by ultrafilter evaluation. If \(\mathcal{U}\) is principal at \(s_{0}\), then \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)=a(s_{0})\), while a free ultrafilter gives a generalised limiting value. For a map \(f\colon S\to T\), we write

\(f(\mathcal{U})=\{A\subseteq T:f^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal{U}\}\)

for the pushforward ultrafilter.

The defining property of the pushforward gives the change-of-variables identity

\(\lim_{s\to\mathcal{U}}b(f(s))=\lim_{t\to f(\mathcal{U})}b(t)\qquad(b\in\ell_{\infty}(T)),\) (2)

which will be the reason for synchronising the pushforwards of the maps used below.

For each integer \(k\geq 1\), choose a finite set \(I_{k}\) so that the sets \(I_{k}\) are pairwise disjoint and \(|I_{k}|\geq k2^{k}\). Set

\(R=\bigsqcup_{k\geq 1}I_{k},\qquad D_{k}=\operatorname{Inj}(\{1,\ldots,k\},I_{k}),\qquad D=\bigsqcup_{k\geq 1}D_{k},\)

where \(\operatorname{Inj}(A,B)\) denotes the set of injective maps from \(A\) to \(B\).

An element \(x\in D_{k}\) may be regarded as an ordered list of \(k\) distinct elements of \(I_{k}\). Define \(f_{n}\colon D\to R\) by

\(f_{n}(x)=\begin{cases}x(n),&x\in D_{k}\text{ and }n\leq k,\\ x(1),&x\in D_{k}\text{ and }n>k.\end{cases}\)

That is, the map \(f_{n}\) reads the \(n\)th entry of \(x\) whenever that entry exists, and otherwise reads its first entry. For each integer \(n\geq 1\), each \(f_{n}\) is finite-to-one: \(f_{n}(D_{j})\subseteq I_{j}\) for every \(j\geq 1\), and the sets \(I_{j}\) are pairwise disjoint. Hence, if \(r\in I_{k}\), then \(f_{n}^{-1}(\{r\})\subseteq D_{k}\), which is finite.

\(f_{n}(\mathcal{U})=\mathcal{V}\qquad(n\geq 1)\)

where \(1_{A_{j}}\) denotes the indicator function of \(A_{j}\). The sets \(C_{\varepsilon}\) partition \(I_{k}\) into at most \(2^{r}\) classes. Hence, by the pigeonhole principle, there is some \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^{r}\) such that

Choose distinct elements \(c_{1},\ldots,c_{k}\in C_{\varepsilon}\), and define \(x\colon\{1,\ldots,k\}\to I_{k}\) by \(x(i)=c_{i}\). Then \(x\in D_{k}\). Moreover, since \(k>K\), we have \(x\notin B_{K}\).

Fix \(1\leq j\leq r\). Since \(n_{j},m_{j}<k\), we have \(f_{n_{j}}(x)=c_{n_{j}}\) and \(f_{m_{j}}(x)=c_{m_{j}}\). Both points belong to \(C_{\varepsilon}\), so

\(1_{A_{j}}(c_{n_{j}})=\varepsilon_{j}=1_{A_{j}}(c_{m_{j}}).\)

Consequently,

\(f_{n_{j}}(x)\in A_{j}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_{m_{j}}(x)\in A_{j},\)

and therefore \(x\notin E(n_{j},m_{j},A_{j})\).

Thus

\(x\notin B_{K}\cup\bigcup_{j=1}^{r}E(n_{j},m_{j},A_{j}).\)

Since the finite collection of generators was arbitrary, no finite union of generators covers \(D\). Hence \(D\notin\mathcal{J}\), and \(\mathcal{J}\) is proper.

Since \(\mathcal{J}\) is proper, the family

\(\mathcal{F}=\{D\setminus J:J\in\mathcal{J}\}\)

is a proper filter on \(D\). Indeed, closure of \(\mathcal{J}\) under finite unions makes \(\mathcal{F}\) closed under finite intersections, closure of \(\mathcal{J}\) under taking subsets makes \(\mathcal{F}\) closed under taking supersets, and properness of \(\mathcal{J}\) ensures that \(\emptyset\notin\mathcal{F}\). By the ultrafilter lemma, extend \(\mathcal{F}\) to an ultrafilter \(\mathcal{U}\) on \(D\). Since \(B_{K}\in\mathcal{J}\), we have \(D\setminus B_{K}\in\mathcal{U}\) for every \(K\geq 1\). Moreover, every finite subset of \(D\) is contained in some \(B_{K}\). Therefore no finite subset of \(D\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\), and hence \(\mathcal{U}\) is free.

For every \(A\subseteq R\) and \(n,m\geq 1\), the complement of \(E(n,m,A)\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\). It follows that

\(f_{n}^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal{U}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f_{m}^{-1}(A)\in\mathcal{U}.\)

Indeed, two sets whose symmetric difference has complement in an ultrafilter must have the same membership in that ultrafilter. Thus all the pushforwards \(f_{n}(\mathcal{U})\) coincide; denote their common value by \(\mathcal{V}\). To see that \(\mathcal{V}\) is free, fix \(n\geq 1\) and suppose that a finite set \(F\subseteq R\) belonged to \(\mathcal{V}=f_{n}(\mathcal{U})\). Then \(f_{n}^{-1}(F)\in\mathcal{U}\) by the definition of pushforward. Since \(f_{n}\) is finite-to-one, this preimage is finite, contradicting the freeness of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Finally, suppose that \(n\neq m\). If \(x\in D_{k}\) with \(k\geq\max\{n,m\}\), then the injectivity of \(x\) gives \(f_{n}(x)\neq f_{m}(x)\). Hence

\(\{x\in D:f_{n}(x)=f_{m}(x)\}\subseteq B_{\max\{n,m\}-1}.\)

The agreement set is therefore finite, so it does not belong to the free ultrafilter \(\mathcal{U}\). ∎

Set

\(\mathscr{M}=\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(R),c_{0}(D)).\)

For \(Q\in\{D,R\}\) and \(h\in\ell_{\infty}(Q)\), let \(M_{h}^{Q}\in\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(Q))\) denote the multiplication operator defined by

\((M_{h}^{Q}z)(q)=h(q)z(q)\qquad(q\in Q).\)

For each integer \(n\geq 1\), define

\(F_{n}(T)=\lim_{x\to\mathcal{U}}e_{x}^{*}Te_{f_{n}(x)}\qquad(T\in\mathscr{M}).\)

The scalar function \(x\mapsto e_{x}^{*}Te_{f_{n}(x)}\) is bounded in modulus by \(\left\lVert T\right\rVert\), so \(F_{n}\) is a well-defined linear functional with \(\left\lVert F_{n}\right\rVert\leq 1\). Thus \(F_{n}\) reads the matrix entry of \(T\) in row \(x\) and column \(f_{n}(x)\) and then takes its \(\mathcal{U}\)-limit. Moreover, for \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(D)\) and \(b\in\ell_{\infty}(R)\), we have

\(F_{n}(M_{a}^{D}TM_{b}^{R})=\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)F_{n}(T)\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)\) (3)

Indeed, the two multiplication operators act on the relevant coordinate vectors by

\(M_{b}^{R}e_{f_{n}(x)}=b(f_{n}(x))e_{f_{n}(x)},\qquad e_{x}^{*}M_{a}^{D}=a(x)e_{x}^{*}.\)

Consequently,

\(e_{x}^{*}M_{a}^{D}TM_{b}^{R}e_{f_{n}(x)}=a(x)\bigl(e_{x}^{*}Te_{f_{n}(x)}\bigr)b(f_{n}(x)),\)

Taking the \(\mathcal{U}\)-limit separates the three scalar factors. The first two limits are \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)\) and \(F_{n}(T)\), while (2) and \(f_{n}(\mathcal{U})=\mathcal{V}\) give

\(\lim_{x\to\mathcal{U}}b(f_{n}(x))=\lim_{r\to\mathcal{V}}b(r)=\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b).\)

This proves (3).

For each integer \(n\geq 1\), define \(S_{n}\colon c_{0}(R)\to c_{0}(D)\) by

\((S_{n}z)(x)=z(f_{n}(x))\qquad(x\in D).\)

If \(z\in c_{0}(R)\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), then

\(\{x\in D:|(S_{n}z)(x)|\geq\varepsilon\}=f_{n}^{-1}(\{r\in R:|z(r)|\geq\varepsilon\}),\)

The set on the right is finite: the level set \(\{r\in R:|z(r)|\geq\varepsilon\}\) is finite because \(z\in c_{0}(R)\), and its preimage is finite because \(f_{n}\) is finite-to-one. Hence \(S_{n}z\in c_{0}(D)\) and \(S_{n}\in\mathscr{M}\). It is immediate that \(\left\lVert S_{n}\right\rVert\leq 1\), and equality follows by taking \(x_{0}\in D\) and \(z=e_{f_{n}(x_{0})}\). The choice of \(S_{n}\) allows the functionals \(F_{m}\) to distinguish the operators \(S_{n}\). Indeed, since \(S_{n}z=z\circ f_{n}\), for each \(x\in D\) we have

\(e_{x}^{*}S_{n}e_{f_{m}(x)}=(S_{n}e_{f_{m}(x)})(x)=e_{f_{m}(x)}(f_{n}(x))=1_{\{y\in D:f_{n}(y)=f_{m}(y)\}}(x).\)

It follows from the definition of \(F_{m}\) that

\(F_{m}(S_{n})=\lim_{x\to\mathcal{U}}1_{\{y\in D:f_{n}(y)=f_{m}(y)\}}(x).\)

If \(m=n\), the function inside the limit is identically one. If \(m\neq n\), Lemma 8.1 shows that its support does not belong to \(\mathcal{U}\), and hence its \(\mathcal{U}\)-limit is zero. Therefore

\(F_{m}(S_{n})=\delta_{m,n}\qquad(m,n\geq 1).\) (4)

We now convert this bounded biorthogonal system into an unbounded functional that satisfies bimodule relations with respect to the characters \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\chi_{\mathcal{V}}\).

There is an unbounded linear functional \(L\colon\mathscr{M}\to\mathbb{K}\) such that

\(L(M_{a}^{D}T)=\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)L(T),\qquad L(TM_{b}^{R})=L(T)\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)\)

for all \(T\in\mathscr{M}\), \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(D)\), and \(b\in\ell_{\infty}(R)\).

Proof.Fold proof

Let \(\mathscr{N}\) be the algebraic subspace

\(\mathscr{N}=\operatorname{span}\{M_{a}^{D}T:\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)=0,\ T\in\mathscr{M}\}+\operatorname{span}\{TM_{b}^{R}:\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)=0,\ T\in\mathscr{M}\}.\)

No closure is taken. Taking \(b=1_{R}\) in (3) gives

\(F_{n}(M_{a}^{D}T)=\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)F_{n}(T),\)

so this expression vanishes whenever \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)=0\). Similarly, taking \(a=1_{D}\) gives

\(F_{n}(TM_{b}^{R})=F_{n}(T)\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b),\)

which vanishes whenever \(\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)=0\). By linearity, every \(F_{n}\) vanishes on \(\mathscr{N}\).

We show that the cosets

\(S_{n}+\mathscr{N}\qquad(n\geq 1)\)

are linearly independent in \(\mathscr{M}/\mathscr{N}\).

Indeed, suppose that for some \(r\geq 1\) and \(c_{1},\ldots,c_{r}\in\mathbb{K}\),

\(\sum_{j=1}^{r}c_{j}(S_{j}+\mathscr{N})=0\)

in \(\mathscr{M}/\mathscr{N}\). Then \(\sum_{j=1}^{r}c_{j}S_{j}\in\mathscr{N}\), and hence, for each \(1\leq m\leq r\),

\(0=F_{m}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{r}c_{j}S_{j}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}c_{j}F_{m}(S_{j})=c_{m}\)

by (4); this shows the desired linear independence.

We may therefore define a linear functional on their linear span by

\(\lambda_{0}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{r}c_{j}(S_{j}+\mathscr{N})\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}jc_{j}.\)

\(\lambda\colon\mathscr{M}/\mathscr{N}\to\mathbb{K}.\)

\(L(S_{n})=n,\qquad\left\lVert S_{n}\right\rVert=1\qquad(n\geq 1),\)

so \(L\) is unbounded.

For \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(D)\) and \(T\in\mathscr{M}\), we have \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a-\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)1_{D})=0\), and therefore

\(M_{a}^{D}T-\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)T=M_{a-\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)1_{D}}^{D}T\in\mathscr{N}.\)

Similarly, for \(b\in\ell_{\infty}(R)\),

\(TM_{b}^{R}-\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)T=TM_{b-\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)1_{R}}^{R}\in\mathscr{N}.\)

Since \(\mathscr{N}=\ker q\subseteq\ker L\), we get

\(L(M_{a}^{D}T)=\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)L(T),\qquad L(TM_{b}^{R})=L(T)\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b),\)

which shows the desired bimodule relation and finishes the proof. ∎

8.1.2.

The incidence algebra

−

It remains to assemble the two diagonal characters and the off-diagonal functional \(L\) into a single homomorphism. For this, we use the height-two poset in which every element of \(D\) lies below every element of \(R\). Its \(c_{0}\)-incidence algebra has exactly the required \(2\times 2\) block form: multiplication operators on the diagonal and the full operator space \(\mathscr{M}\) in the upper-right corner.

Let \(\mathcal{P}=D\sqcup R\), ordered by retaining equality and declaring

\(d<r\qquad(d\in D,\ r\in R).\)

This is a countable poset. Relative to \(c_{0}(\mathcal{P})=c_{0}(D)\oplus_{\infty}c_{0}(R)\), Definition 6.9 gives

\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}M_{a}^{D}&T\\ 0&M_{b}^{R}\end{pmatrix}:a\in\ell_{\infty}(D),\ b\in\ell_{\infty}(R),\ T\in\mathscr{M}\right\}.\) (5)

Indeed, distinct elements of \(D\) are incomparable, as are distinct elements of \(R\), so both diagonal blocks are multiplication operators. The block from \(c_{0}(D)\) to \(c_{0}(R)\) must vanish, while the block from \(c_{0}(R)\) to \(c_{0}(D)\) is unrestricted.

Define

\(\Phi\colon\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\to\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K}),\qquad\Phi\left(\begin{pmatrix}M_{a}^{D}&T\\ 0&M_{b}^{R}\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)&L(T)\\ 0&\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)\end{pmatrix}.\)

This is an algebra homomorphism. Indeed, let

\(A=\begin{pmatrix}M_{a}^{D}&T\\ 0&M_{b}^{R}\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}M_{a^{\prime}}^{D}&S\\ 0&M_{b^{\prime}}^{R}\end{pmatrix}.\)

The diagonal entries of \(\Phi(AB)\) agree with those of \(\Phi(A)\Phi(B)\) because \(\chi_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\chi_{\mathcal{V}}\) are characters. The upper-right block of \(AB\) is \(M_{a}^{D}S+TM_{b^{\prime}}^{R}\), and Lemma 8.2 gives

\(L(M_{a}^{D}S+TM_{b^{\prime}}^{R})=\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)L(S)+L(T)\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b^{\prime}),\)

which is the upper-right entry of \(\Phi(A)\Phi(B)\).

The map \(\Phi\) is surjective because, for all \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb{K}\),

\(\Phi\left(\begin{pmatrix}M_{\alpha 1_{D}}^{D}&\beta S_{1}\\ 0&M_{\gamma 1_{R}}^{R}\end{pmatrix}\right)=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ 0&\gamma\end{pmatrix}.\)

It is discontinuous because

\(A_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&S_{n}\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}\qquad(n\geq 1)\)

satisfies \(\left\lVert A_{n}\right\rVert=1\), whereas

\(\Phi(A_{n})=\begin{pmatrix}0&n\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix}\)

has norm \(n\).

We shall also need the following elementary observation.

Let \(K_{0}\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space, let \(K\) be its one-point compactification, and let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a Banach algebra. Suppose that

\(\Psi\colon\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{0}))\to\mathscr{C}\)

is an algebra homomorphism whose kernel contains every finite-rank operator on \(C_{0}(K_{0})\). Then there is an algebra homomorphism

\(\widetilde{\Psi}\colon\mathscr{B}(C(K))\to\mathscr{C}\)

having the same range as \(\Psi\). Moreover, \(\widetilde{\Psi}\) is continuous if and only if \(\Psi\) is continuous, and it is compact if and only if \(\Psi\) is compact. In particular, surjectivity and discontinuity are preserved by this lifting.

Proof.Fold proof

Identify \(C_{0}(K_{0})\) with the closed subspace of functions in \(C(K)\) that vanish at \(\infty\). Let \(\jmath\colon C_{0}(K_{0})\to C(K)\) be the canonical inclusion, let \(u=1_{K}\), and define \(\varepsilon\in C(K)^{*}\) and \(\pi\colon C(K)\to C_{0}(K_{0})\) by

\(\varepsilon(f)=f(\infty),\qquad\pi(f)=f-\varepsilon(f)u\qquad(f\in C(K)).\)

Using the vector-first convention for rank-one operators, we have \(\pi\jmath=I_{C_{0}(K_{0})}\) and

\(I_{C(K)}=\jmath\pi+u\otimes\varepsilon.\)

Define

\(\widetilde{\Psi}(T)=\Psi(\pi T\jmath)\qquad(T\in\mathscr{B}(C(K))).\)

For \(T,S\in\mathscr{B}(C(K))\), we have

\(\pi TS\jmath=(\pi T\jmath)(\pi S\jmath)+(\pi Tu)\otimes(\varepsilon S\jmath).\)

The second summand has rank at most one and therefore belongs to \(\ker\Psi\). Hence \(\widetilde{\Psi}(TS)=\widetilde{\Psi}(T)\widetilde{\Psi}(S)\).

Define

\(\iota\colon\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{0}))\to\mathscr{B}(C(K)),\qquad\iota(A)=\jmath A\pi.\)

Since \(\pi\jmath=I_{C_{0}(K_{0})}\), the map \(\iota\) is a bounded algebra homomorphism and

\(\widetilde{\Psi}(\iota(A))=\Psi(A)\qquad(A\in\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{0}))).\)

Since every value of \(\widetilde{\Psi}\) is also a value of \(\Psi\), the two homomorphisms have the same range.

The map \(T\mapsto\pi T\jmath\) is bounded, so continuity and compactness of \(\Psi\) imply the corresponding properties of \(\widetilde{\Psi}\). Conversely, \(\Psi=\widetilde{\Psi}\circ\iota\), and \(\iota\) is bounded, so continuity and compactness of \(\widetilde{\Psi}\) imply the corresponding properties of \(\Psi\). ∎

We are now ready for the construction of the desired discontinuous homomorphism.

Proof of Theorem 1.8.Fold proof

Apply Theorem 1.5 to the sequence

\(\mathscr{C}_{1}=\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0}),\qquad\mathscr{C}_{n}=\{0\}\qquad(n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}).\)

We obtain an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\), a bounded surjective algebra homomorphism

\(\theta\colon\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\longrightarrow\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0}),\)

and an isometric algebra-homomorphic right inverse

\(\rho\colon\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\)

such that \(\theta\circ\rho\) is the identity on \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\). Moreover,

\(\ker\theta=\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})).\)

Set \(\Psi=\Phi\circ\theta\). Since both \(\Phi\) and \(\theta\) are surjective, so is \(\Psi\). If \(\Psi\) were continuous, then \(\Phi=\Psi\circ\rho\) would be continuous, contradicting the construction of \(\Phi\). Thus \(\Psi\) is a discontinuous surjective algebra homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) onto \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\).

Let \(K\) be the one-point compactification of \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\). Since

\(\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))=\ker\theta\subseteq\ker\Psi,\)

every finite-rank operator on \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) belongs to \(\ker\Psi\). Lemma 8.3 therefore gives an algebra homomorphism

\(\widetilde{\Psi}\colon\mathscr{B}(C(K))\longrightarrow\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\)

having the same range as \(\Psi\). Hence \(\widetilde{\Psi}\) is surjective, and it is discontinuous because continuity is preserved in both directions by the lifting.

Finally, the points \(x_{n}\) indexed by \(\mathbb{N}\) are isolated in \(K\), and

\(K^{\prime}\subseteq\{y_{A}:A\in\mathcal{A}\}\cup\{\infty\}.\)

Each \(y_{A}\) is isolated in \(K^{\prime}\), so \(K^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\{\infty\}\) and \(K^{\prime\prime\prime}=\emptyset\). Thus \(K\) is compact, scattered, and has Cantor–Bendixson height at most three. ∎

8.2.

Possible quotient algebras and ideal counts

−

Theorem 1.5 gives a large supply of quotient algebras of the form \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\). In this final subsection, we determine the finite ideal counts obtained from the building blocks in that theorem and give some concrete examples. We also show that the construction can produce the largest possible number of maximal closed ideals.

If \(\mathscr{C}\) is a Banach algebra, let \(\mathfrak{I}(\mathscr{C})\) denote the lattice of closed two-sided ideals of \(\mathscr{C}\), including \(\{0\}\) and \(\mathscr{C}\) itself. For a finite partially ordered set \(\mathcal{P}\), write

\(\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{P})=\{(s,t)\in\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}:s\leq t\},\)

ordered by containment of intervals,

\((s,t)\preceq(u,v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\leq s\leq t\leq v.\)

Set

\(N(\mathcal{P})=|\operatorname{Up}(\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{P}))|,\)

where \(\operatorname{Up}(\mathcal{Q})\) denotes the family of upsets of a partially ordered set \(\mathcal{Q}\). By , the lattice of two-sided ideals of \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) is naturally anti-isomorphic to the lattice of order ideals of \(\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{P})\). Since \(\mathcal{P}\) is finite, all these ideals are closed, and since complementation identifies order ideals with upsets,

\(N(\mathcal{P})=|\mathfrak{I}(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}))|.\)

Each finite-poset factor is assumed to be nonempty.

The finite numbers of non-trivial closed ideals furnished by Theorem 1.5 are precisely the integers of the form

\(3^{r}\prod_{i=1}^{k}N(\mathcal{P}_{i}),\)

where \(\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{k}\) are finite partially ordered sets and \(r,k\geq 0\). If \(r+k\geq 1\), then, for each such choice, the corresponding algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) may be chosen to have exactly

\(r+\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\mathcal{P}_{i}|\)

maximal closed ideals. In the exceptional case \(r=k=0\), the corresponding algebra may be chosen to be \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\), which has one non-trivial closed ideal, and this ideal is also its unique maximal closed ideal.

Proof.Fold proof

If \(r=k=0\), apply Theorem 1.5 to the identically zero sequence. As in the proof of that theorem, we may take \(\mathcal{A}=\emptyset\), so that \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})=c_{0}\). The algebra \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\) has precisely three closed ideals,

\(\{0\},\qquad\mathscr{K}(c_{0}),\qquad\mathscr{B}(c_{0}).\)

Thus it has exactly one non-trivial closed ideal, which is also its unique maximal closed ideal. We may therefore suppose that \(r+k\geq 1\).

First, apply Theorem 1.5 to a sequence whose non-zero terms are

\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}_{1}),\ldots,\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}_{k})\)

together with \(r\) copies of \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\). We obtain an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\) such that

\(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\cong\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}_{i})\right)\times\mathscr{B}(c_{0})^{r}.\)

The closed ideals of a finite product of unital Banach algebras are precisely the products of closed ideals in the coordinates. Each algebra \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}_{i})\) has \(N(\mathcal{P}_{i})\) closed ideals, while \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\) has exactly three closed ideals . Hence the quotient has

\(3^{r}\prod_{i=1}^{k}N(\mathcal{P}_{i})\)

closed ideals. Proposition 1.3 gives the same number of non-trivial closed ideals in \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\). Indeed, passing from the ideals of the quotient to the non-trivial ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) removes the whole algebra and adds the missing ideal \(\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\), so the number is unchanged.

Conversely, suppose that

\(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\)

is a quotient algebra furnished by Theorem 1.5 and has only finitely many closed ideals. If this product is zero, then its lattice of closed ideals has one element, and Proposition 1.3 gives exactly one non-trivial closed ideal in the corresponding operator algebra. We may therefore suppose that the quotient is non-zero.

Since the quotient has only finitely many closed ideals, its non-zero factors are matrix algebras, finite incidence algebras, and copies of \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\); an infinite \(c_{0}\)-incidence algebra is excluded because the diagonal characters \(T\mapsto e_{t}^{*}Te_{t}\) have pairwise distinct maximal kernels. Each matrix algebra has exactly two closed ideals, a contribution already represented by a one-point poset. Since the number of closed ideals of a finite product is the product of the numbers of closed ideals of its factors, the stated form follows.

For the maximal-ideal count, shows that for a finite poset \(\mathcal{P}\) the maximal ideals of \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) are precisely

\(\{f\in\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}):f(t,t)=0\}\qquad(t\in\mathcal{P}).\)

Thus \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) has exactly \(|\mathcal{P}|\) maximal ideals. The algebra \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\) has a unique maximal closed ideal, and a maximal ideal of a finite product is obtained by choosing a maximal ideal in one coordinate and taking the whole algebra in every other coordinate. Hence the quotient constructed above has

\(r+\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\mathcal{P}_{i}|\)

maximal ideals. Proposition 1.3 transfers these maximal ideals to \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\). ∎

It remains to identify concrete values of \(N(\mathcal{P})\); the product formula then supplies arbitrary finite products of these values, together with arbitrary powers of \(3\). Let us spell out some examples.

If \(\mathcal{P}\) is an antichain with \(d\) points, then \(\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{P})\) is an antichain with \(d\) points, so

\(N(\mathcal{P})=2^{d}.\)

Thus every power of \(2\) is obtained. If \(\mathcal{P}\) is a chain with \(d\) points, then the upsets of \(\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{P})\) are counted by the Catalan number \(C_{d+1}\), giving

\(2,5,14,42,132,\ldots.\)

The values arising from height-two posets admit a useful general formula. Let \(G=(L\sqcup R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, where \(L\sqcup R\) stands for the vertex set of the graph and \(E\) for its edges. Let \(\mathcal{P}_{G}\) be the poset on the disjoint union \(L\sqcup R\) defined by

\(\ell<r\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\ell\in L,\ r\in R,\ \text{and }(\ell,r)\in E.\)

For \(I\subseteq L\) and \(J\subseteq R\), write

\(e_{G}(I,J)=|E\cap(I\times J)|.\)

For every finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\sqcup R,E)\),

\(N(\mathcal{P}_{G})=\sum_{I\subseteq L}\sum_{J\subseteq R}2^{e_{G}(I,J)}.\)
Proof.Fold proof

The elements of \(\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal{P}_{G})\) are the diagonal intervals \((v,v)\), for \(v\in L\sqcup R\), together with the intervals \((\ell,r)\) corresponding to the edges \((\ell,r)\in E\). The only non-trivial order relations are

\((\ell,\ell)\preceq(\ell,r)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(r,r)\preceq(\ell,r).\)

Let \(\mathcal{W}\) be an upset, and let \(I\subseteq L\) and \(J\subseteq R\) consist of those vertices \(v\) for which \((v,v)\notin\mathcal{W}\). Once \(I\) and \(J\) are fixed, every edge interval having at least one endpoint outside \(I\sqcup J\) is forced to belong to \(\mathcal{W}\). The remaining edge intervals correspond to the \(e_{G}(I,J)\) edges between \(I\) and \(J\), and each may be included independently. Thus there are \(2^{e_{G}(I,J)}\) upsets with these prescribed missing diagonal intervals. Summing over \(I\) and \(J\) proves the formula. ∎

If \(G=K_{p,q}\) is complete bipartite, Proposition 8.5 gives

\(N(\mathcal{P}_{K_{p,q}})=\sum_{i=0}^{p}\sum_{j=0}^{q}\binom{p}{i}\binom{q}{j}2^{ij}=\sum_{i=0}^{p}\binom{p}{i}(1+2^{i})^{q}.\)

For \(p=1\), this gives

\(N(\mathcal{P}_{K_{1,q}})=2^{q}+3^{q}\)

and hence we obtain the values

\(5,13,35,97,\ldots.\)

For \(p=2\), we have

\(N(\mathcal{P}_{K_{2,q}})=2^{q}+2\cdot 3^{q}+5^{q},\)

which yields

\(47,187,803,\ldots\)

for \(q=2,3,4,\ldots\). Similar constructions yield further values, and arbitrary finite products of these values are also obtainable. However, this does not appear to cover all the natural numbers, so Question 1.11 remains open.

We observe that we can also obtain the largest possible number of maximal closed ideals for an algebra of cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\).

There is an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) has exactly \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\) maximal closed ideals.

Proof.Fold proof

Apply Theorem 1.5 with \(\mathscr{C}_{n}=\mathbb{K}\) for every \(n\). The resulting quotient is

\(\ell_{\infty}=C(\beta\mathbb{N}).\)

Its maximal ideals are the kernels of evaluation at the points of \(\beta\mathbb{N}\), and \(|\beta\mathbb{N}|=2^{\mathfrak{c}}\). Proposition 1.3 therefore gives the same number of maximal closed ideals in \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\). ∎

Let us finally indicate the scope of the construction. Theorem 1.5 realises countable normed products of the listed building blocks, but it does not characterize all Banach algebras that can occur as such quotients. Accordingly, Proposition 8.4 describes the ideal counts furnished by this construction, rather than all possible counts arising from arbitrary almost disjoint families.

toc.title: An overview of matrices acting on almost disjoint families.
Possible quotient algebras and ideal counts

results.statementHtml:
Suppose that \(\mathcal{P}\) is a partially ordered set which admits an order embedding into \(\wp(\mathfrak{c})\). Then there exist a collection \((\mathcal{A}_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) of uncountable, almost disjoint families \(\mathcal{A}_{t}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) and a collection of isometric algebra homomorphisms \(\iota_{s,t}:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{t}})\) for \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\) with \(s\leq t\) such that:

  1. (a)

    \(\iota_{s,s}\) is the identity on \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\), and \(\iota_{s,t}\iota_{r,s}=\iota_{r,t}\) for all \(r\leq s\leq t\).

  2. (b)

    Let \(T:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{s}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{t}})\) be an operator for some \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\). Then

    • –

      if \(s\leq t\), then \(T=\lambda\iota_{s,t}+S\), where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\) and \(S\) is an operator that factors through \(c_{0}\),

    • –

      if \(s\not\leq t\), then \(T\) factors through \(c_{0}\).
There are \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\) pairwise non-isomorphic spaces of the form \(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\), where \(\mathcal{A}\) is an almost disjoint family of cardinality \(\mathfrak{c}\).

Let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) be an almost disjoint family. The ideal \(\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) of compact operators is the smallest non-zero closed ideal of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) and if \(\varphi:\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\to\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) denotes the quotient map, then

\(\mathscr{J}\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathscr{J})\)

is a lattice isomorphism between the lattice of closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) and the closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) strictly larger than \(\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\).

Let \(\mathfrak{J}\) denote the lattice of closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\), then the previous proposition can be succinctly described by saying that the lattice of closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is given by

\(\{0\}\subsetneq\mathscr{K}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\subsetneq\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{J}).\)

Let \((\mathscr{C}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq\mathfrak{A}\). Then there exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) and a short exact sequence

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

which splits strongly. Furthermore, the continuous right inverse \(\rho\) may be chosen to be an isometry, and \(\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert=1\) whenever \(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\neq\{0\}\).

Here “splits strongly” is understood in the sense of Definition 2.2; in particular, there is a continuous algebra homomorphism \(\rho\colon\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\to\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) such that \(\theta\circ\rho\) is the identity map on \(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mathscr{C}_{n}\). Equivalently, if zero factors are allowed, the one-factor case can be viewed as the product with \(\mathscr{C}_{1}=\mathscr{C}\) and \(\mathscr{C}_{n}=\{0\}\) for \(n\geq 2\).

Let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a finite-dimensional, semi-simple complex algebra. Then there exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))/\mathscr{X}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is isomorphic to \(\mathscr{C}\).

There exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that there is a discontinuous surjective algebra homomorphism

\(\Psi\colon\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\longrightarrow\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K}),\)

where \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\) denotes the algebra of upper-triangular \(2\times 2\) scalar matrices. Consequently, there exist a compact scattered Hausdorff space \(K\) of Cantor–Bendixson height at most three and a discontinuous surjective algebra homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))\) onto \(\mathbb{T}_{2}(\mathbb{K})\).

Theorem 1.8 does not control derivations from the same operator algebra. Following the arguments in , we believe that, under \((\mathsf{CH})\), it should be possible to construct an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\) such that every derivation from \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) is continuous while the algebra admits a discontinuous homomorphism into a Banach algebra. Establishing these two properties simultaneously would require a substantially longer argument.

For the unique maximal ideal assertion, assume K is nonempty.

Let \(C(K)\) be separable. Then \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))\) has a unique maximal ideal. Moreover, there exists some \(n\in\{2,3\}\) such that the space of operators on any separable \(C(K)\)-space never has exactly \(n\) non-trivial closed ideals.

Correction in this reading edition

K is understood to be nonempty in the unique maximal ideal assertion. The zero algebra has no proper maximal ideal.

For which \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(n\geq 1\), does there exist an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that the operator algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) contains exactly \(n\) non-trivial closed ideals?

A sequence of Banach algebra homomorphisms

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{I}\xlongrightarrow{\jmath}\mathscr{B}\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\mathscr{C}\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

is called short exact if \(\jmath\) is injective, \(\theta\) is surjective and \(\ker\theta=\jmath(\mathscr{I})\). In the applications below, \(\jmath\) will be the inclusion map, and we shall identify \(\mathscr{I}\) with its image in \(\mathscr{B}\).

A short exact sequence

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{I}\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\mathscr{C}\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

is called strongly split if there is a continuous algebra homomorphism \(\rho\colon\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{B}\) such that \(\theta\circ\rho\) is the identity map on \(\mathscr{C}\). In this case, \(\rho\) is called a continuous right inverse for \(\theta\).

For every infinite ordinal \(\alpha\), the algebra of operators on \(C(\alpha)\) has a unique maximal ideal. In particular, if \(C(\alpha)\not\sim C(\xi\cdot n)\) for any uncountable regular cardinal \(\xi\) and \(n\in\mathbb{N},n\geq 2\) then the set \(\mathcal{M}_{C(\alpha)}(C(\alpha))\) is the unique maximal ideal of \(\mathscr{B}(C(\alpha))\).

The case \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\omega_{1})\), or more generally \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\omega_{\eta})\) where \(\eta\) is any ordinal such that \(\omega_{\eta}\) is a regular cardinal, was already shown by Kania and Laustsen , while the case \(C(\alpha)\sim C(\beta)\) for \(\beta\) a countable epsilon number, that is, a countable ordinal satisfying \(\omega^{\beta}=\beta\), was shown by Philip A. H. Brooker (unpublished).

Assume K is nonempty.

Let \(K\) be a compact metric space. Then \(\mathscr{B}(C(K))\) admits a unique maximal ideal.

Correction in this reading edition

K is nonempty here. The statement about a unique maximal ideal fails for the zero function space.

The algebra of operators on \(C(\omega^{\omega^{2}})\) has at least four non-trivial closed ideals. Consequently, there exists some \(n\in\{2,3\}\) such that the space of operators on any separable \(C(K)\)-space never has exactly \(n\) non-trivial closed ideals.

Let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) be an almost disjoint family. We define the topological space \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) consisting of distinct points \(\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\cup\{y_{A}:A\in\mathcal{A}\}\), where \(x_{n}\) is isolated for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and the sets

\(U(A,F)=\{x_{n}:n\in A\setminus F\}\cup\{y_{A}\}\)

for finite \(F\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) form a neighbourhood basis at each point \(y_{A}\) for \(A\in\mathcal{A}\). We will write \(U(A)\) for \(U(A,\emptyset)\).

results.statementHtml: Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) is an almost disjoint family and \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) is a separable subspace. Then there exists a closed subspace \(\mathcal{Y}\subseteq C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) such that \(\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\sim c_{0}\).

Suppose that \((\mathcal{A}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is a sequence of almost disjoint families \(\mathcal{A}_{n}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\). Then there exists an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{B}\) such that \(K_{\mathcal{B}}\) is homeomorphic to the topological sum \(\coprod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}K_{\mathcal{A}_{n}}\). In particular, we have

\(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\cong C_{0}\left(\coprod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}K_{\mathcal{A}_{n}}\right)\cong\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}_{n}})\right)_{c_{0}}.\)

Let \(L\) be an open subset of a locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\). Then the map \(\tau\colon\alpha K\to\alpha L\) given by

\(\tau(k)=\begin{cases}k&\text{if }k\in L\\ \infty_{L}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\)

is a continuous surjection, and hence the induced map \(\tau^{\circ}_{0}\colon C_{0}(L)\to C_{0}(K)\) is an isometric algebra homomorphism.

Lemma 4.6 does not imply that \(\alpha L\) is a retract of \(\alpha K\). The reason is that \(\alpha L\) may not be a topological subspace of \(\alpha K\) because the map \(\alpha L\to\alpha K\) which is the identity on \(L\) and maps \(\infty_{L}\) to \(\infty_{K}\) may be discontinuous at \(\infty_{L}\). This explains why we distinguish the points at infinity by adding the subscripts \(K\) and \(L\) to them.
Let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) be almost disjoint families. Then \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) is an open subset of \(K_{\mathcal{B}}\).

By Lemmas 4.6 and 4.8 the induced map \(\tau_{0}^{\circ}:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\) is an isometric algebra homomorphism. We refer to it as the canonical embedding and denote it with the symbol \(\iota\). Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) are almost disjoint families. To avoid confusion, we will denote the isolated points of \(K_{\mathcal{B}}\) by \(\{z_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\); that is \(K_{\mathcal{A}}=\{x_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\cup\{y_{A}:A\in\mathcal{A}\}\) and \(K_{\mathcal{B}}=\{z_{n}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\cup\{y_{B}:B\in\mathcal{B}\}\). Then \(\iota:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\) can be explicitly described, for any \(f\in C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\), by

\((\iota f)(z_{n})=f(x_{n}),\qquad(\iota f)(y_{A})=\begin{cases}f(y_{A}),&\text{if }A\in\mathcal{A},\\ 0,&\text{if }A\in\mathcal{B}\setminus\mathcal{A}.\end{cases}\)

Further, observe that if we have nested almost disjoint families \(\mathcal{A}_{r}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{s}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{t}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) then the corresponding canonical embeddings satisfy \(\iota_{s,t}\iota_{r,s}=\iota_{r,t}\).

Let \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) be an almost disjoint family and \(B\in\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that \(B\not\in\mathcal{A}\) and \(\{B\}\cup\mathcal{A}\) is an almost disjoint family. Then for any \(f\in C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\) we have \(\lim_{k\in B}f(x_{k})=0\).

Let \(M=(m_{k,n})_{k,n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be a matrix with entries in \(\mathbb{K}\). We define

  • •

    \(\mathbb{M}=\{M:\left\lVert M\right\rVert<\infty\}\) where \(\left\lVert M\right\rVert=\sup\{\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}|m_{k,n}|:k\in\mathbb{N}\}\).

  • •

    For \(f\in\ell_{\infty}\) and \(M\in\mathbb{M}\) we define \(Mf\in\ell_{\infty}\) by \(Mf(k)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}m_{k,n}f(n)\) for \(k\in\mathbb{N}\).

  • •

    We let \(I\) denote the \(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\) identity matrix and for \(A\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) we denote by \(1_{A}\in\ell_{\infty}\) the indicator function of the set \(A\).

Suppose that \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) are almost disjoint families, \(C,D\in\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\), and \(M\in\mathbb{M}\). We say that:

  • •

    \(\left(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\right)\) admits \(M\) if \(\lim_{k\in B}(M1_{A})(k)=0\) for every \(A\in\mathcal{A}\), \(B\in\mathcal{B}\). If \(\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\), we will say that \(\mathcal{A}\) admits \(M\).

  • •

    \((C,D)\) rejects \(M\) if \(\lim_{k\in D}(M1_{C})(k)\) does not exist. If \(C=D\), we will say that \(C\) rejects \(M\).

  • •

    \(C\) undermines \(M\) if there is \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(((M1_{\{n\}})(k))_{k\in C}\) does not converge to \(0\).

Suppose that \(M\in\mathbb{M}\) and that \(A,B\in\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}.\)

  • •

    For \(j\in\mathbb{N}\), we define \(M_{j}=(m^{\prime}_{k,n})_{k,n\in\mathbb{N}}\) where \(m^{\prime}_{k,n}=0\) if \(n\leq j\) and \(m^{\prime}_{k,n}=m_{k,n}\) otherwise.

  • •

    We say that \(M\) is a compact matrix if \(\lim_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\left\lVert M_{j}\right\rVert=0\).

  • •

    We define \(M^{A}_{B}=(m^{\prime}_{k,n})_{k,n\in\mathbb{N}}\), where \(m^{\prime}_{k,n}=m_{k,n}\) if \((k,n)\in B\times A\), and \(m^{\prime}_{k,n}=0\) otherwise.

  • •

    We say that \((A,B)\) accepts \(M\) if \(M^{A}_{B}\) is a compact matrix.

  • •

    Finally, for families \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) we say that \((\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\) accepts \(M\) if \((A\cup A^{\prime},B\cup B^{\prime})\) accepts \(M\) for every \(A,A^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}\), \(B,B^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}\). If \(\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}\), we say that \(\mathcal{A}\) accepts \(M\).

We note that our formulation of \(\mathcal{A}\) accepting \(M\) is formally stronger than that of Koszmider and Laustsen. However, using Monotonicity , the reader can readily verify that the two formulations are in fact equivalent.

Let \(M\in\mathbb{M}\) and \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\). Suppose that \((\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\) accepts \(M\).

  1. (1)

    (Admission) If no \(B\in\mathcal{B}\) undermines \(M\), then \((\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\) admits \(M\).

  2. (2)

    (Monotonicity) Suppose that \(C\in\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) is contained in a finite union of elements of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(D\in\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) in a finite union of elements of \(\mathcal{B}\). Then \((C,D)\) accepts \(M\).

Let \(K,L\) be scattered, locally compact Hausdorff spaces and \(T:C_{0}(K)\to C_{0}(L)\) be an operator. Then the reduced matrix of \(T\) is the matrix \(M^{r}_{T}=(m_{z,x})_{z\in L\setminus L^{\prime},x\in K\setminus K^{\prime}}\) given by \(m_{z,x}=T^{*}\delta_{z}(\{x\})\) for \(x\in K\setminus K^{\prime}\), \(z\in L\setminus L^{\prime}\), where recall that \(K\setminus K^{\prime}\) and \(L\setminus L^{\prime}\) denote the set of isolated points of \(K\) and \(L\) respectively.

Let \(K,L\) be infinite, scattered, locally compact Hausdorff spaces, and let \(F=K\setminus K^{\prime}\) and \(G=L\setminus L^{\prime}\) be the sets of isolated points. Suppose \(T:C_{0}(K)\to C_{0}(L)\) is an operator. Then \(K^{\prime}\) contains a set \(E\) of cardinality not bigger than the cardinality of \(G\) such that

\(T(f)|G=M^{r}_{T}(f|F)\)

whenever \(f\in C_{0}(K)\) and \(f(y)=0\) for every \(y\in E\).

Suppose that \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) are almost disjoint families and that \(T:C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}})\to C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{B}})\) is an operator.

  1. (a)

    There exists \(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\) countable such that for all \(A\in\mathcal{A}\setminus\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\) and every \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) we have

    \(T1_{U(A)}(z_{k})=(M^{r}_{T}1_{A})(k).\)

    Consequently, no \((A,B)\in(\mathcal{A\setminus A^{\prime}})\times\mathcal{B}\) rejects \(M^{r}_{T}\).

  2. (b)

    If there exist countable subsets \(\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{B}\) such that \((\mathcal{A}\setminus\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime},\mathcal{B}\setminus\mathcal{B}^{\prime\prime})\) admits \(M^{r}_{T}\), then \(T\) factors through \(c_{0}\).
