results.title: (A dichotomy for acceptance and rejection ).
results.statementHtml:
Suppose that \(M\in\mathbb{M}\) and \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) is an uncountable, almost disjoint family such that \(\{1_{A}:A\in\mathcal{A}\}\) is a Borel subset of \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\). Then one of the following holds:

  1. (a)

    either \(\mathcal{A}\setminus\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\) accepts \(M-\lambda I\) for some countable \(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\),

  2. (b)

    or there are pairwise disjoint sets \(\{A_{\xi},A^{\prime}_{\xi}\}\subseteq\mathcal{A}\) and an infinite subset \(B_{\xi}\subseteq A_{\xi}\cup A^{\prime}_{\xi}\) such that \(B_{\xi}\) rejects \(M\) for every \(\xi<\mathfrak{c}\).

Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a partially ordered set. We say that a family \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) of Banach spaces has few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}\) if the following are satisfied for \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\):

  1. (a)

    \(X_{t}\) is not separable.

  2. (b)

    If \(s\leq t\) then there exists an isometric embedding \(\iota_{s,t}:X_{s}\to X_{t}\) so that every operator \(T:X_{s}\to X_{t}\) is of the form \(T=\lambda\iota_{s,t}+S\), where \(\lambda\in\mathbb{K}\) and \(S\) has separable range. Furthermore, for every \(r\leq s\leq t\) we have \(\iota_{s,t}\iota_{r,s}=\iota_{r,t}\).

  3. (c)

    If \(s\not\leq t\), then every operator \(T:X_{s}\to X_{t}\) has separable range.

We think of the spaces \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) as being nested relative to the poset \(\mathcal{P}\). Accordingly, whenever we write \(X_{s}\subseteq X_{t}\) for \(s\leq t\), we implicitly identify \(X_{s}\) with its image \(\iota_{s,t}(X_{s})\subseteq X_{t}\).
In case (c), that is, whenever \(s\nleq t\), we adopt the convention of defining \(\iota_{s,t}=0\) to maintain consistency in the notation.

Let \((\mathcal{P},\leq)\) be a locally finite partially ordered set. The incidence algebra of \(\mathcal{P}\) is the algebra

\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})=\{f\colon\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{K}:f(s,t)=0\text{ for }s,t\in\mathcal{P}\text{ with }s\not\leq t\},\)

with the sum of functions and scalar multiplication defined pointwise. The product \(h=f\star g\) is defined via convolution

\(h(s,t)=\sum_{s\leq r\leq t}f(s,r)g(r,t).\)

For technical reasons, we will work with the incidence algebra on the poset with the opposite order \(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}}\). Observe that this algebra can be explicitly described in terms of the original order as

\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}})=\{f\colon\mathcal{P}\times\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{K}:f(s,t)=0\text{ for }s,t\in\mathcal{P}\text{ with }t\not\leq s\},\)

and the product becomes

\((f\star g)(s,t)=\sum_{t\leq r\leq s}f(s,r)g(r,t).\)

Assume the poset is nonempty.

Suppose that \(\mathcal{P}\) is a finite partially ordered set, \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}}\) is a family that has few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}\) and \(Y=\bigoplus_{t\in\mathcal{P}}X_{t}\). Assume moreover that the spaces \(X_{t}\) contain a common non-separable subspace \(Z\), and that \(\iota_{t,s}\) restricts to the identity on \(Z\) whenever \(t\leq s\). Then

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{X}(Y)\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}(Y)\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}})\longrightarrow\{0\}\)

is a strongly split exact sequence, the right inverse \(\rho\) of \(\theta\) is an isometry and \(\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert=1\).

Correction in this reading edition

The norm-one assertion requires a nonempty poset. For the empty direct sum the map has norm zero.
Given a finite partially ordered set \(\mathcal{P}\), is the incidence algebra \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) a Calkin algebra?
Let \((\mathcal{P},\leq)\) be a locally finite partially ordered set. Then the incidence algebra \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P})\) is normable if and only if \(\mathcal{P}\) is finite.

The \(c_{0}\)-incidence algebra \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\) is the subspace of \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(\mathcal{P}))\) given by operators \(T\) satisfying \(e^{*}_{s}Te_{t}=0\) whenever \(s\not\leq t\) for \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\).

We observe that, in principle, one can define \(E\)-incidence algebras similarly for any Banach space \(E\) with an unconditional basis. However, since such algebras are not well-suited to our purposes, we will not pursue this direction.
\(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\) is a closed subalgebra of \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(\mathcal{P}))\).

Let \(\mathcal{P}=\mathbb{N}\) with the usual order \(\leq\). Then \(\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P},c_{0})\) is the subalgebra of operators on \(c_{0}\) that have upper-triangular matrix representation. Similarly, if we take \(\mathcal{P}=\mathbb{N}\) with the opposite order relation \(\geq\), we get the algebra of operators that have lower-triangular matrix representation.

We define the bounded extension of \(\mathcal{P}\) to be the poset \((\mathcal{P}^{*},\leq)\) where we adjoin two formal extra elements \(\mathcal{P}^{*}=\mathcal{P}\cup\{0,\infty\}\) and declare \(s\leq t\) whenever \(t=\infty\), or \(s=0\) or \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\) and \(s\leq t\).

Let \(\Lambda=(\lambda_{s,t})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\) be an infinite scalar matrix. We say that \(\Lambda\) has \(\ell_{1}\)-bounded rows if

\(\sup_{s\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{P}}|\lambda_{s,t}|<\infty.\)

We say that \(\Lambda\) has \(c_{0}\)-columns if for every \(t\in\mathcal{P}\) we have \((\lambda_{s,t})_{s\in\mathcal{P}}\in c_{0}(\mathcal{P})\).

1. (a)

    Let \(T\in\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(\mathcal{P}))\). Then \((\lambda_{s,t})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\), the scalar matrix of \(T\), has \(\ell_{1}\)-bounded rows and \(c_{0}\)-columns. Moreover,

    \(\left\lVert T\right\rVert=\sup_{s\in\mathcal{P}}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{P}}|\lambda_{s,t}|.\)
  2. (b)

    Let \(\Lambda=(\lambda_{s,t})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\) be an infinite scalar matrix having \(\ell_{1}\)-bounded rows and \(c_{0}\)-columns. Then there exists an operator \(T\in\mathscr{B}(c_{0}(\mathcal{P}))\) with \(\Lambda\) as its scalar matrix.

As in the case of incidence algebras, for technical reasons, it will be convenient to work with the \(c_{0}\)-incidence algebra in the opposite order. In terms of the original order, this means that the subalgebra of operators is defined by the condition \(e_{s}^{*}Te_{t}=0\) whenever \(t\nleq s\) for \(s,t\in\mathcal{P}\). Note that, since the underlying set is unchanged, we have \(c_{0}(\mathcal{P})=c_{0}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}})\).

Let \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}^{*}}\) be a family of Banach spaces with few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\), and set \(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{t\in\mathcal{P}}X_{t}\right)_{c_{0}}\). Then the map \(\rho:\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}},c_{0})\to\mathscr{B}(Y)\), sending an operator \(T\) with scalar matrix \(\Lambda=(\lambda_{s,t})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\) to the operator with matrix \((\lambda_{s,t}\iota_{t,s})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\) defines an isometric homomorphism.

Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces and \(S_{n}:X\to Y\) be an operator with separable range for each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Suppose that \(S_{n}\to S\) in the strong operator topology. Then \(S\) has separable range.

Let \((X_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \((Z_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) be sequences of Banach spaces, \(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}X_{n}\right)_{c_{0}}\), \(W=\left(\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb{N}}Z_{n}\right)_{c_{0}}\) and \(S=(S_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\in\mathscr{B}(Y,W)\). Then \(S\) has separable range if and only if \(S_{n,m}\) has separable range for each \(n,m\in\mathbb{N}\).

Let \(\mathscr{B}\) and \(\mathscr{C}\) be algebras over \(\mathbb{K}\), and let \(\mathscr{I}\) be an ideal of \(\mathscr{B}\). Suppose that \(\theta:\mathscr{B}\to\mathscr{C}\) is a linear map with \(\ker\theta=\mathscr{I}\). If \(\theta\) admits a multiplicative right inverse \(\rho:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{B}\), then \(\theta\) is multiplicative.

Let \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}^{*}}\) be a family of Banach spaces with few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\), and set \(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{t\in\mathcal{P}}X_{t}\right)_{c_{0}}\). Then for any operator \(T=(T_{s,t})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\in\mathscr{B}(Y)\), the matrix \(\Lambda=(\lambda_{s,t})_{s,t\in\mathcal{P}}\), where \(T_{s,t}=\lambda_{s,t}\iota_{t,s}+S_{s,t}\) with \(\lambda_{s,t}\in\mathbb{K}\) and \(S_{s,t}\) has separable range, corresponds to an operator \(\theta(T)\in\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}},c_{0})\).

Moreover, the map

\(\theta:\mathscr{B}(Y)\to\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}},c_{0}),\hskip 5.0ptT\mapsto\theta(T)\)

is an algebra homomorphism with \(\left\lVert\theta\right\rVert=1\) and \(\ker\theta=\mathscr{X}(Y)\).

Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a countable partially ordered set and let \((X_{t})_{t\in\mathcal{P}^{*}}\) be a family of Banach spaces with few operators relative to \(\mathcal{P}^{*}\). Set

\(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{t\in\mathcal{P}}X_{t}\right)_{c_{0}}.\)

Then there is a strongly split short exact sequence

\(\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathscr{X}(Y)\longrightarrow\mathscr{B}(Y)\xlongrightarrow{\theta}\operatorname{\mathbf{IA}}(\mathcal{P}^{\operatorname{op}},c_{0})\longrightarrow\{0\}.\)

The previous proposition, together with Theorem 1.1, enables the construction of many subalgebras of the infinite-dimensional triangular matrices as quotients of \(\mathscr{B}(X)\), thereby providing a partial answer to . It also yields algebras of upper and lower-triangular matrices as quotients of \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) for suitable Banach spaces \(X\), offering alternative solutions to , distinct from the one obtained in .

There are free ultrafilters \(\mathcal{U}\) on \(D\) and \(\mathcal{V}\) on \(R\) such that

\(f_{n}(\mathcal{U})=\mathcal{V}\qquad(n\geq 1)\)

and

\(\{x\in D:f_{n}(x)=f_{m}(x)\}\notin\mathcal{U}\qquad(n,m\geq 1,\ n\neq m).\)

There is an unbounded linear functional \(L\colon\mathscr{M}\to\mathbb{K}\) such that

\(L(M_{a}^{D}T)=\chi_{\mathcal{U}}(a)L(T),\qquad L(TM_{b}^{R})=L(T)\chi_{\mathcal{V}}(b)\)

for all \(T\in\mathscr{M}\), \(a\in\ell_{\infty}(D)\), and \(b\in\ell_{\infty}(R)\).

Let \(K_{0}\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space, let \(K\) be its one-point compactification, and let \(\mathscr{C}\) be a Banach algebra. Suppose that

\(\Psi\colon\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{0}))\to\mathscr{C}\)

is an algebra homomorphism whose kernel contains every finite-rank operator on \(C_{0}(K_{0})\). Then there is an algebra homomorphism

\(\widetilde{\Psi}\colon\mathscr{B}(C(K))\to\mathscr{C}\)

having the same range as \(\Psi\). Moreover, \(\widetilde{\Psi}\) is continuous if and only if \(\Psi\) is continuous, and it is compact if and only if \(\Psi\) is compact. In particular, surjectivity and discontinuity are preserved by this lifting.

Each finite-poset factor is assumed to be nonempty.

The finite numbers of non-trivial closed ideals furnished by Theorem 1.5 are precisely the integers of the form

\(3^{r}\prod_{i=1}^{k}N(\mathcal{P}_{i}),\)

where \(\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{k}\) are finite partially ordered sets and \(r,k\geq 0\). If \(r+k\geq 1\), then, for each such choice, the corresponding algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) may be chosen to have exactly

\(r+\sum_{i=1}^{k}|\mathcal{P}_{i}|\)

maximal closed ideals. In the exceptional case \(r=k=0\), the corresponding algebra may be chosen to be \(\mathscr{B}(c_{0})\), which has one non-trivial closed ideal, and this ideal is also its unique maximal closed ideal.

Correction in this reading edition

The finite-poset factors are taken to be nonempty. The formalisation treats zero factors and the exceptional empty product separately.

For every finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\sqcup R,E)\),

\(N(\mathcal{P}_{G})=\sum_{I\subseteq L}\sum_{J\subseteq R}2^{e_{G}(I,J)}.\)
There is an almost disjoint family \(\mathcal{A}\subseteq\left[{\mathbb{N}}\right]^{\omega}\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_{0}(K_{\mathcal{A}}))\) has exactly \(2^{\mathfrak{c}}\) maximal closed ideals.

proposition-1-3.note: compact c0 factorisation and finite-rank approximation prove compact minimality; noncompact scattered-C0 factorisation and a complemented c0 copy identify ideals strictly above compact with those containing the separable kernel; the Banach quotient order isomorphism is the exact printed inverse-image map, including empty/countable families

remark-1-4.note: direct consequence of the concrete definitions and the already proved constructions; no additional mathematical assumption

theorem-1-5.note: paper disjoint-poset construction with shared bounds; all four admissible component splittings and zero components are assembled into the actual bounded product; flattening and relabeling the dependent c0 sum gives one actual Mrowka space with the exact separable kernel, isometric multiplicative section and nonzero-product norm-one clause

remark-1-6.note: direct consequence of the concrete definitions and the already proved constructions; no additional mathematical assumption

corollary-1-7.note: finite-dimensional complex semisimple algebra classification, followed by the proved Theorem 1.5; the resulting quotient is the actual Banach quotient algebra, including the zero algebra

theorem-1-8.note: the proved ultrafilter bimodule functional gives a discontinuous triangular incidence homomorphism; Theorem 1.5 and the finite-rank-annihilating compactification lift realize it on the specified C(K), with the exact range and third-derived-set bound

remark-1-9.note: This is a conjectural discussion. The completed formalisation does not claim to prove the conjecture.

proposition-1-10.note: separability of C(K) implies compact metrizability by a countable separating family; exact Corollary 3.3 and Proposition 3.4 give both assertions, with the approved nonempty convention explicit

question-1-11.note: This is an open question in the paper. The formalisation does not claim to settle it.

proposition-3-1.note: all ordinal cases proved: regular and singular initial blocks, finite powers, countable ranked Wolfe selection, and arbitrary-cofinality principal ranks. Actual ceiling correction, full-cardinality coloured cores, cofinal reindexing and local inverses factor an original complementary operator with uniform bounds; genuine ordinal classification transports preserve the regular finite-copy exception.

remark-3-2.note: regular initial ordinals and all countable ordinals, hence countable epsilon numbers, are already proved

corollary-3-3.note: finite compact case, countable compact ordinal classification and proved countable ordinal primary factorisation, and the Milutin uncountable compact metric case; the nonempty convention is explicit

proposition-3-4.note: the explicit Alspach surjection has Wolfe extinction below omega squared at every positive scale; the proved necessary factorisation criterion contradicts identity factorisation.
